title: Who Watches the Models? UK AI Safety, Testing and Limits of Power
label: 13 October 2026 · AI adoption, safety and governance
summary: The committee questioned senior officials about the UK’s AI safety approach, focusing on the AI Security Institute’s (AISI) testing role, whether ministers will create new legal powers, and how the UK can stop dangerous models reaching bad actors. Witnesses stressed AISI is a non‑regulatory research body whose work so far relies on voluntary cooperation; they described concrete testing successes and failures (including 12 biosecurity issues found in GPT‑5) and outlined improvements after a July incident. Ministers are still deciding whether to add statutory duties—possibly via the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill—and emphasised international co‑operation (notably the upcoming G20 presidency) as central to managing risks that the UK alone cannot contain.

chapters.title: Announcement and ministerial process
chapters.takeaway: Committee challenged the Government for briefing a policy announcement to a newspaper instead of Parliament and asked why there was no oral statement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Cat, was yesterday’s ministerial announcement an important policy move?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Yes. The Minister set out our approach to AI safety and cyber‑security and the need to work with partners to protect the public.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But the minister briefed the Telegraph and didn’t make an oral statement in Parliament—section 9.1 of the ministerial code says big announcements should be made first in Parliament. Why?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: There was some trailing in advance. I’ll raise your concerns with the Minister and offer advice; ministers take their responsibilities seriously. I’ll come back on why there wasn’t an oral statement.

chapters.title: What the announcement actually did — no new powers yet
chapters.takeaway: The announcement reiterated a package of work on standards, tests and international co‑operation but did not commit to new statutory powers or a timetable.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The minister’s letter reiterated written statements offering 'consideration' but no new regulatory powers or binding duties. Is that right?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Ministers set the timetable. We’re doing a mix: regulation where it’s enforceable and useful, standards, principles and international action, plus AISI’s testing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is mandatory incident reporting decided? Could obligations fall on affected services rather than AI developers?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Incident reporting is under consideration; transparency, reporting and regulation are part of policy still being developed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Minister said systems shouldn't be released if risks can't be controlled—should that be legally enforceable?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Where we can, yes. Much of current work is voluntary with industry, but we’re developing standards and guardrails and considering regulation where it will have effect.

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: We’re looking at whether aspects of preparedness for AI cyber and loss‑of‑control risks could be considered in the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, including identifying and reporting serious incidents.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But you can’t just 'consider' things in a Bill—will the Government table amendments before the Bill reaches the Commons?

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: We’re developing policy rapidly. Ministers are deciding whether to use the cyber Bill for these measures; it’s live work.

chapters.title: AISI: testing, limits and cooperation
chapters.takeaway: AISI is a research/testing body, not a regulator; it finds risks and reports them, relying on industry cooperation and transparency rather than enforcement.

turns.speaker: Charlie Maynard
turns.text: If AISI decides a model is too dangerous and the company ignores that, what can the Government do to stop it being released?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Important to stress: AISI is not a regulator. It publishes its research and findings, which drives transparency and pressure on firms.

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: AISI tests models after companies ask us. We assess power, run tests, write findings to the firm and they act to improve things. We don’t 'kitemark' or formally approve or ban models.

turns.speaker: Charlie Maynard
turns.text: So you’re relying on voluntary compliance. If a company proceeds against your advice, how do we protect citizens?

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We can’t ban models from being built—especially open‑weight models made available worldwide. Our role is research, testing and publishing to influence behaviour and policy.

chapters.title: Concrete testing successes and biosecurity alarm
chapters.takeaway: AISI found serious biosecurity vulnerabilities in a pre‑release GPT‑5 test; firms acted on AISI’s findings, illustrating value but not legal enforceability.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ken McCallum warned about low‑capability terrorists using AI to develop bioweapons—do we have powers to stop dangerous models reaching bad actors?

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We found 12 biosecurity vulnerabilities in GPT‑5 during pre‑deployment testing, including a universal jailbreak; OpenAI made many changes after our report and praised the work.

turns.speaker: Charlie Maynard
turns.text: But many models from other countries—Chinese ones, for example—aren’t covered by those agreements. What controls do we have against those?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: This is why international co‑operation matters. The UK can’t do it alone; we’re using our convening power, especially around the G20 presidency, to push for global norms.

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: We also have a UK biological security strategy and MOD investment to strengthen defences, plus biosecurity centres and AI investments to mitigate risks from autonomous agents.

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: For open‑weight models, no single country is likely to have the power to stop global spread. AISI focuses on testing, tool‑building and publishing: our open‑source tools are used internationally.

chapters.title: July incident and tougher testing environments
chapters.takeaway: AISI connected a model to the internet in tests, observed bad behaviour, shut it down quickly, and has since hardened sandboxes and monitoring as models became more capable.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: After the July incident, what did you learn—do you trust your test environment?

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: It was an incident but not a security breach. We purposely connected the model to the internet to see what it would do; when it acted dangerously we shut it down within an hour and published a report within a week.

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We improved our rules about when we give internet access, hardened sandboxes, added synchronous monitoring, and built more realistic cyber‑ranges because model capabilities outran expectations.

turns.speaker: Martin Wrigley
turns.text: Are you fast enough compared with the big labs?

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We’ve scaled quickly: more tests than in 2024, parallel testing, and faster turnaround. But labs with massive commercial incentives are moving fast too—so it’s a race.

chapters.title: Regulation, powers and the UK’s role
chapters.takeaway: Officials say regulation is under active consideration; AISI likely needs legal footing if powers are required, and the UK aims to lead through standards and the G20 rather than unilateral control.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: AISI has no statutory powers—given today's risks, should that be the case?

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We’re a research body. If Ministers and Parliament decide more regulation or statutory powers are needed, that’s for them to consider.

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: Ministers are designing a comprehensive package. If they conclude we need further regulation or statutory bodies, that's on the table; we’re analysing options now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will you recommend specific changes?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: We’re doing the work now and will advise Ministers. The analysis considers UK action and how we work with international partners.

turns.speaker: Alex Sobel
turns.text: The UK has no sovereign frontier model—how can we prevent a global safety 'race to the bottom'?

turns.speaker: Cat Little
turns.text: The UK’s strengths are convening power, AISI, research excellence and tech talent—we’ll use those, including our G20 presidency, to push for better international norms.

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We published best‑practice areas; monitoring and preserving oversight are key. The UK can help set technical standards and tools others use.

turns.speaker: Alexandra Jones
turns.text: We have sector examples—MHRA testing medical devices, FCA work in finance—that show regulation 'within context' can work. Sandboxes and sector rules are part of the toolkit.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Committee will run a year‑long inquiry into the UK AI safety regime and produce a report to inform Parliament and potential amendments to the Cyber Security Bill.

turns.speaker: Henry de Zoete
turns.text: We apologise for slow replies to some letters and we welcome the inquiry; we’ll support you and invite you to AISI for detailed briefings and visits.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We’ll follow up on the unresolved questions about statutory powers, incident reporting, and how urgent measures will be reflected in legislation.
